report:
**Conclusion: yes—probably, but the benefit is modest and product-specific certainty is limited.** For women with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis (usually recurrent symptomatic, culture-confirmed lower UTI), regular cranberry products reduce recurrence on average compared with placebo/no cranberry. The strongest synthesis is the 2023 Cochrane review, which found benefit particularly in women with recurrent UTIs. The plausible mechanism is cranberry proanthocyanidins reducing *E. coli* attachment to bladder cells—not treating an established infection.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321_cranberries-preventing-urinary-tract-infections

This does **not** mean any cranberry juice or extract will reliably work. Trials used juice, concentrates, tablets, and extracts with widely varying proanthocyanidin (PAC) content, doses, adherence, and outcome definitions. Thus, the evidence supports *trying a standardized cranberry product as a non-antibiotic preventive option*, rather than asserting that ordinary cranberry juice universally prevents cystitis. It is not a substitute for evaluation or antibiotics when infection is present.

Guidelines reflect that nuance: the American Urological Association discusses cranberry as prophylaxis for recurrent uncomplicated UTI and notes studies of juice, concentrate, and dried extract but inconsistent dosing.  
https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/recurrent-uti

The evidence applies poorly to complicated UTIs, catheter users, pregnancy, or people with urinary-tract abnormalities; those situations need clinician guidance. Cranberry products are generally well tolerated, but juice can add substantial sugar/calories, and people taking warfarin should check with their prescriber because interaction evidence is conflicting.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/cranberry
